title: Reading the history
objectives: Read git log and find a commit by its message
Read git diff line by line
Undo unstaged edits and bring back an older version of a file

screens.prose:
Your backtest's signal used to average 20 days of prices. Now it averages 50. You ask Git for the history, one line per commit:

```sh
$ git log --oneline
```

rows: e52f9c1 Use a 50-day moving average for the signal

screens.question: Tap the commit that made that change.

hints.text: Read the messages. Which one mentions the signal?
Only one message says what it changed to the signal.
e52f9c1's message names the 50-day moving average.

feedback.correct: The message says exactly what changed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the message that mentions the signal.

byKey.r3c0: "fix" might be anything. You would have to open it to know, and the clear message is two lines up.
byKey.r1c0: "wip" means work in progress. It says nothing about the signal.
byKey.r0c0: This one added trading costs, as its message says.

explain.text: You found it from the message alone, without opening a single commit. "fix", "stuff" and "wip" would each have to be opened and read. Each line starts with the commit's hash, its short name.

screens.prose: `git log` lists every commit in the project. `HEAD -> main` marks the commit you are on now.

rows: e52f9c1 Use a 50-day moving average for the signal

screens.question: Tap the first commit ever made in this project.

hints.text: Which commit is HEAD, where you are now?
HEAD marks the newest commit.
HEAD is on the top line, so the newest is at the top. The first commit is at the bottom.

feedback.correct: The log lists the newest first, so the oldest is at the bottom.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where HEAD is, then go the other way.

byKey.r0c0: You tapped the top line, as if the log read like a diary. It lists the newest commit first; HEAD is on it.

explain.text: HEAD, your current commit, is on top, so the log runs from newest to oldest. The first commit, "Add daily returns script", is at the bottom. Read a log upwards to follow the story in time order.

screens.prose: You raise the trading cost in `backtest.py` from 5 bp to 10 bp per trade, and stage it. Next month you will scan this log for it.

rows: e52f9c1 Use a 50-day moving average for the signal

screens.question: Which commit message is best?

options.text: Raise trading cost from 5 bp to 10 bp per trade

options.why: Git already records which file changed. The message should say what changed in it.
You wrote the kind of message you could not use on the first screen. It says nothing about the change.

options.text: Change costs, tidy the plot and rename variables
options.why: This describes three changes. They belong in three commits, each with its own message.

hints.text: Which message would let you find this commit without opening it?
These messages forced you to guess.
Say what changed, in a short line that starts with a verb. Leave which files to Git.

feedback.correct: It says what changed, and you could find it by reading the log.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the message you could search for next month.

explain.text: A good message is a short line saying what the commit changes, starting with a verb. Git records the files already. One change per commit keeps each message honest.

screens.prose:
Before committing, you check what you changed since the last commit. Each line carries a mark: a minus, a plus or none.

```sh
$ git diff backtest.py
```

state.caption: Lines 12 to 14 of backtest.py. No mark: unchanged.

screens.question: Tap the line that is no longer in the file.

hints.text: Which mark could mean taken away?
These two lines carry a mark.
Minus marks a line taken out; plus marks a line put in. Lines with no mark are unchanged context.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the mark at the start of each line.

byKey.r3c1: The plus line is the new one, now in the file. Its partner with a minus is the one removed.
byKey.r1c1: This line has no mark: unchanged, shown for context.
byKey.r4c1: This line has no mark: unchanged, shown for context.
byKey.r0c1: The @@ line is a header saying where in the file the change is.

explain.text: `-` marks a line removed and `+` a line added; lines with no mark are unchanged context. Here `.shift(1)` was removed: each day's position now uses that same day's close. That is lookahead, and the backtest will look far too good.

screens.prose: You undo that edit, then change only one number: the 20 becomes a 50. `git diff` prints this, and later `git commit` will report "1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)".

state.caption: No mark: an unchanged line, shown for context

screens.question: How many lines of the file did you edit?

widget.label: Lines edited
widget.accept: 1: a changed line shows as one minus and one plus.

hints.text: Compare the minus line with the plus line. How much differs?
These two lines are nearly identical.
Git has no mark for a changed line. It shows the old line removed and the new one added: one edit, two marked lines.

feedback.correct: One line edited, shown as a removal and an addition.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what differs between the two marked lines.

byKey.two: You counted the two marked lines as two edits. They are the old and new versions of one line.
byKey.three: You counted the context line too. It has no mark, so it is unchanged.

explain.text: Git has no mark for a changed line. It shows the old version removed and the new version added. So one edited line always appears as a minus and a plus.

screens.prose:
Happy with the 50-day signal, you stage it and check again:

```sh
$ git add backtest.py
$ git diff
$
```
screens.question: `git diff` printed nothing. What happened?

options.text: `git diff` compares the working folder with the staging area, and they now match
The edit was lost when you staged it
options.why: Staging copies the file; it never deletes your edit. v2 is in both places.
`git add` only stages. The last commit still holds v1.

options.text: `git diff` only works after a commit
options.why: It worked a moment ago, before the `git add`. What changed is which places match.

hints.text: Which two places does plain `git diff` compare?
These two columns now hold the same version.
Plain git diff shows unstaged changes: working against staged. Both are v2, so there is nothing to show. git diff --staged compares staged with the last commit.

feedback.correct: Nothing unstaged is left, so plain `git diff` is empty.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which two places `git diff` compares.

byKey.lost: You took the empty output to mean the edit vanished. It is staged, so it no longer counts as unstaged.
byKey.committed: You took staging as committing. The last commit is still v1.

explain.text: Plain `git diff` shows only unstaged changes: working folder against staging area. To see what you are about to commit, run `git diff --staged`, which compares the staging area with the last commit. Here that shows the 20 becoming 50.

screens.prose: Later you try a new idea in `returns.py`, nothing staged. It breaks everything. You want the file back exactly as it was in the last commit.
screens.question: Which commands put `returns.py` back as it was? Select all that apply.

options.why: That stages the broken version. It is the opposite of what you want.
--staged acts on the staging area, which already holds v2. Your broken working copy stays as it is.
`git log` only reads the history. It changes no file.

hints.text: You want to copy the good version over your working copy. Which commands write to the working folder?
Your broken copy is here.
`git restore returns.py` copies the staged v2 over it. `git checkout -- returns.py` is the older spelling of the same thing.

feedback.correct: Both copy the good version over your broken one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the commands that overwrite your working copy.

byKey.add: You picked `git add`. It would stage the broken version, not undo it.

explain.text: `git restore returns.py` copies the staged version over your working copy; `git checkout -- returns.py` is the older command for the same thing. Your broken edits are gone for good, since they were never committed. Use it only on edits you truly want to throw away.

screens.prose:
The commands that read the history, and the one that undoes an edit:

```sh
$ git log --oneline
$ git diff
$ git diff --staged
$ git restore returns.py
```

The log lists the newest first. Plain diff shows unstaged changes; `--staged` shows what the next commit holds.
screens.question: You want to check exactly what your next commit will contain. Which command?

options.why: Plain diff shows what you have not staged. You saw it print nothing after `git add`.
The log lists commits already made, not the one you are about to make.

hints.text: The next commit holds what is staged. Which command compares the staging area with the last commit?
`git diff --staged` compares the staging area with the last commit.

feedback.correct: It shows the staged changes, which are what the commit records.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the empty diff after `git add`.

explain.text: A commit records the staging area, and `git diff --staged` shows how that differs from the last commit. Reading it before every commit catches the stray change. Plain `git diff` shows what would be left behind.

screens.prose: Yesterday at 18:00 your backtest ran cleanly at commit `4b8d0a3`. Three commits today broke `backtest.py`, and you cannot see where. You decide to bring back yesterday's file and record that as a new commit.

rows: d71f0b2 (HEAD -> main) Vectorise the P&L loop
8a2c4e9 Read prices with dates as index
e52f9c1 Use a 50-day moving average for the signal

state.caption: Today's three commits are at the top

screens.question: Put the steps in order.

lines.text: `python backtest.py`, to check it runs cleanly

hints.text: You need the hash before you can use it.
Find the hash, bring back the file, check it works, then commit. `git checkout <hash> -- file` also stages the file.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step needs the one before it.

explain.text: `git checkout 4b8d0a3 -- backtest.py` copies yesterday's file into your folder and stages it, so the commit needs no `git add`. Today's three commits stay in the history. Later you can diff each of them to find the bug.

ideas: `git log` lists the newest commit first. A message that says what changed lets you find a commit without opening it.
In a diff, minus is a line removed, plus a line added, space unchanged. A changed line shows as one of each.
`git restore file` throws away unstaged edits; `git checkout <hash> -- file` brings back an older version.

formula.name: What git diff compares
formula.tex: \begin{aligned} \texttt{git diff} &: \text{working vs staged} \\ \texttt{git diff -{}-staged} &: \text{staged vs last commit} \end{aligned}

summary.trap: An empty `git diff` after `git add` does not mean the edit is lost. It is staged; use `git diff --staged`.

quiz.prose:
`git log --oneline` prints:

```
b2e9a71 (HEAD -> main) Add stop-loss
77c0d3f Charge 5 bp per trade
1fa8e20 Load SPY prices
```
quiz.question: Which commit came straight after "Load SPY prices"?

options.why: You read the log top to bottom as time order. The newest is on top, so the order in time runs upwards.

options.text: None: it is the newest commit
options.why: HEAD is on the top line, so the top is newest. Load SPY prices is the oldest.

feedback.correct: The log runs newest first, so the next commit in time is the line above.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find HEAD first.

explain.text: HEAD marks the newest commit, on top. Reading upwards gives time order: Load SPY prices, then Charge 5 bp per trade, then Add stop-loss.

quiz.question: How many lines does the file have in this part after the change?

widget.label: Lines after the change
widget.accept: 4: two context lines and two plus lines.

feedback.correct: Two unchanged lines and two added lines.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the lines with a space or a plus.

byKey.all: You counted the minus line too. It was removed, so it is not in the file now.
byKey.three: You left out a context line or a plus line. Every line not marked minus is in the new file.

explain.text: The new file holds the context lines and the plus lines: 2 + 2 = 4. The header agrees: `+3,4` means four lines from line 3.

quiz.prose: You run `git restore signal.py` on a file with an hour of unstaged, uncommitted edits. Then you change your mind.
quiz.question: Can Git bring those edits back?

options.text: No: Git never had a copy of them

options.why: The log holds only commits. Those edits were never committed.
The staging area never held those edits either. They were only in your working copy.

feedback.correct: Unstaged, uncommitted edits exist only in your file.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where Git could have kept a copy.

explain.text: Git keeps copies only of what you stage or commit. `git restore` overwrote the only copy of that hour's work. Commit, or at least stage, before you experiment.
